site.title: Data Skunkworks
site.description: Interactive data visualisations by Thomas Colin, each with a short note on how it was made and a link to its code.
site.headline: Experiments with data.
site.lede: Each project below has a short note on how I built it and a link to the code, so you can make your own.
about: I'm Thomas Colin, a data scientist in Brisbane. I've spent my career turning data into information, most recently at Atlassian.
Data Skunkworks is where the experiments live: each piece starts with a question and ends with something you can poke at.
The code for every piece is on [GitHub](https://github.com/thomasc91/dataskunkworks).

pieces.title: Brisbane pixel diorama
pieces.summary: A 3D pixel-art model of inner Brisbane, built from open map data, that you can fly around.
pieces.standfirst: Every building within 5 km of West End, from the CBD towers to the Queenslanders, on the real hills, with live CityCats, trains, buses and planes, cars and cyclists at real traffic levels, and the real sun and weather.
facts: OpenStreetMap, Overture Maps, Queensland's LiDAR elevation model, TransLink, Brisbane City Council, Open-Meteo and adsb.lol
57,008 buildings, 136,000 trees and 14 hand-built bridges in a 5 km circle, plus the airport
three.js r170 and WebGL, with Claude

p: Drag to orbit, scroll to zoom, and hover or click a building to see its height and floors. The sun slider moves the shadows from 6am to 5:15pm, and the photo view frames Eagle Street.

The CityCats, ferries, trains, buses and Metro sit at their real GPS positions, and the planes are the real flights passing over Brisbane, so hover any of them to see where it's headed. The cars are simulated, but how many are out follows the council's live traffic signal data, and the cyclists ride the bikeways in the numbers its bike counters record.
The Airport button opens a second map of Brisbane Airport, where you can watch the planes land, take off and taxi to the gates.
In daylight the sun and the weather follow the real time in Brisbane, so the shadows and the clouds are today's.
Buildings and hills are drawn 1.6 times taller than they really are, so the skyline still reads from a distance.

The model is one data file: 57,008 building footprints with heights, the trees, 14,304 road segments, the parks and the river, all clipped to a circle 5 km around West End. three.js draws it in WebGL, and the pixel finish, labels and traffic can each be switched off.

The ground follows Queensland's bare-earth LiDAR elevation model, sampled every 10 m, so Mt Coot-tha and the inner-city hills rise out of the map. The river bridges are hand-built models drawn from published dimensions and photos.
The railway comes from OpenStreetMap, and each train follows the track between its GPS fixes, through the junctions, over the bridges and into the tunnels.
The live ferries, trains, buses and planes come through a small relay on Cloudflare, which fetches each feed every few seconds and shares it with everyone who has the map open.
It was built with Claude in October 2026.

Buildings, streets, parks and the railway are © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL) and the Overture Maps Foundation. The elevation is the State of Queensland's QldDem (CC BY-SA), the ferry, train and bus positions are TransLink's open GTFS-RT feed (CC BY 4.0), the traffic signal data and bike counts are Brisbane City Council's (CC BY 4.0), the weather is Open-Meteo's, and the aircraft positions are [adsb.lol](https://adsb.lol/) open data.
The map files come to 14 MB, so give it a few seconds on a phone.

pieces.title: London pixel diorama
pieces.summary: A 3D pixel-art model of central London, with its landmarks built by hand, that you can fly around.
pieces.standfirst: Every building within 5 km of the South Bank, from the City towers to the terraces of Kennington, with Big Ben, the Shard, Tower Bridge and ten more landmarks modelled to their real shapes.
facts: 91,694 buildings, 86,430 trees and 13 hand-built landmarks in a 5 km circle
three.js r170 and WebGL, with Claude

p: Drag to orbit, scroll to zoom, and hover or click a building to see its height and floors. The sun slider moves the shadows across an October day in London, and the skyline view frames the towers of the City.
The cars, buses, Thames ferries and planes are simulated, not live. Buildings are drawn 1.6 times taller than they really are, so the skyline still reads from a distance.

Thirteen landmarks are hand-built models placed on their real footprints: Elizabeth Tower and Victoria Tower, Westminster Abbey, the London Eye, St Paul's Cathedral, the Shard, Tower Bridge, the White Tower, the Gherkin, the Walkie-Talkie, the Cheesegrater, the BT Tower and Battersea Power Station.
Their shapes and sizes follow published dimensions. The London Eye is scaled evenly so its wheel stays round, and St Paul's dome keeps its real proportions.

It uses the renderer from the Brisbane pixel diorama with a new pipeline that can build any city from open map data: Overture Maps for the buildings and their heights, and OpenStreetMap for the river, parks, trees, roads, bridges and ferries. Where a building has no mapped height, it's estimated from its neighbours or its type, and its card says so.
It was built with Claude in October 2026.
Buildings, streets and parks are © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL) and the Overture Maps Foundation. The model file is 20 MB, so give it a few seconds on a phone.

pieces.title: The Dying of the Dragons
pieces.summary: A hand-drawn, scrolling map of the Targaryen civil war, in which the sky slowly empties of dragons.
pieces.standfirst: Twenty dragons flew over Westeros at the start of 129 AC. Two years of civil war later, four were left. Scroll through the war and watch it happen.
facts: A Wiki of Ice and Fire (CC BY-SA 3.0)
Canvas and ES modules, no libraries, with Claude

p: A map of the war's theatre in ink and wash. Twenty-one dragons fly the war's routes at their relative sizes, and 37 people move, change sides and die across 14 steps. Scroll or use the arrow keys to move through the story, hover any dragon, person or place for its fate, and press M for the maester's notes.

Every event, rider, death, place and size follows [A Wiki of Ice and Fire](https://awoiaf.westeros.org/index.php/Dance_of_the_Dragons), checked page by page. Sizes keep the ratios the wiki gives, so Vhagar is five times the length of Arrax. Of the 37 people on the map, 25 die during the war.

Every line comes from a small hand-drawn canvas engine, first written for a redraw of Florence Nightingale's rose diagram, with no libraries. Built with Claude in September 2026. It's a non-commercial fan work, not affiliated with George R. R. Martin or HBO, and it uses no imagery from the television series.

pieces.title: Game of Thrones networks
pieces.summary: Who matters in A Song of Ice and Fire, as force-directed networks of the characters in all five books.
pieces.standfirst: Two characters are linked when their names appear within 15 words of each other. Pick a book and watch the web of Westeros settle.

p: One network per book. Each node is a character, sized by how central they are, and each line joins two characters who appear close together in the text. Click a book to load it, drag nodes around, scroll to zoom, and click and hold a character to fade everyone they aren't connected to.

In A Game of Thrones, Eddard Stark is the hub, with 66 connections and the highest centrality. A Storm of Swords is the densest book, with 303 characters and 1,008 links. By A Dance with Dragons the centre has moved to Jon Snow.

D3's force layout, with zoom and drag. The networks come from Andrew Beveridge's [asoiaf repository](https://github.com/mathbeveridge/asoiaf), built for the [Network of Thrones](https://networkofthrones.wordpress.com/) research with Jie Shan.

pieces.title: Every James Bond vehicle
pieces.summary: A scrolling story of every scene Bond spends in a car, plane, boat or train, across 25 films and 60 years.
pieces.standfirst: 492 scenes and about 14 hours of Bond behind the wheel, in the cockpit or at the helm. Scroll, and the scenes regroup to answer a new question at each step.
facts: D3 v5 force layout and a scroll-driven story

p: Each circle is one scene in a vehicle, sized by how long it lasts and coloured by air, land or sea. As you scroll, the circles regroup: by element, by actor, by Bond's most-used vehicles and by class. Hover a circle for the film, the vehicle and the minutes on screen.

The Spy Who Loved Me (1977) spends 53% of its running time in vehicles, the most of any film, while Dr. No spends 9%. The 1964 Aston Martin DB5 turns up in 22 scenes across 8 films, including four of Daniel Craig's five.
D3 with a force layout that sends every circle to a new target at each scroll step, on Cuthbert Chow's scroller. The scene data was provided by Koen Van den Eeckhout.
